extracted.intended_audience: herbalists, apothecaries, gardeners, cooks, fishermen and natural philosophers (early-modern practitioners)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical instructions and evaluative guidance for propagating plants, selecting and preparing edible and medicinal plant parts, preserving fruits/vegetables/herbs, identifying safe fungi, capturing animals/fish, and related domestic/culinary-apothecary operations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grafting/propagation effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Plants change when grafted with foreign stock: branches introduced from another tree produce different leaves and fruits; grafting can cause variation and degeneration in genera.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the host trunk is appropriate (e.g., 'truncus ipse precifus fuerit'); be aware that fruits from grafted branches can be markedly different from the original tree. Watch for degeneration (e.g., 'quercus genus degenerat') and for cases where age causes female plants to degenerate. Use proper timing and sites for inserting grafts to avoid undesirable mutations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Select plant parts by temperament for desired odor/effect
rubrics_metrics.description: The nature (hot/cold, humid/dry) of a plant determines its odor and therapeutic/palatability properties: 'odores enim frigidi magis anima recreat'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For sweeter, more pleasant odors and soothing effects choose plants with 'cold' qualities; for stronger purgative or heating effects choose warmer plants. Consider that constitution affects cerebral response ('cerebrum calore affildo'). Use knowledge of plant temperament when choosing for perfuming, medicinal, or culinary aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drying flowers and leaves (degree of dryness)
rubrics_metrics.description: When drying herbs/flowers for storage or scent, the degree of dryness matters: moderate drying preserves flavors/odors; excessive desiccation causes loss of desirable properties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If material is too dry it will 'excidiffent' (fall away) and lose substance; slightly drying (brief heating or sun exposure) and then storing preserves scent and later use. If drying for sweet preserves or oils, avoid over-drying to retain combined flavors/odors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods for preserving fruits and vegetables
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple preservation techniques are prescribed: boiling in water or wine, salting, sugaring (maceration and repeated cooking with sugar), pickling in vinegar, sun-drying in shade, or storage in oil/olive brine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedures: macerate in water until soft, dry in shade, then boil repeatedly with sugar to make candied fruits; for olives and similar fruits wash, dry, salt or boil and then keep in cool places; cucumbers and melons can be boiled in wine to prevent spoilage and then stored in cool, shaded places. Monitor humidity and avoid incomplete drying (which leads to mold).

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of roots and herb parts for curing/preservation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prefer sturdier, somewhat thicker roots ('venioxum duriora') for preservation and medicinal preparations; more tender parts behave differently when cured.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When intending to preserve roots or use them medicinally, select parts of the right firmness; prepare with vinegar, pepper, cloves and other aromatics before drying. Remember that overly thin or over-dried pieces lose flavor and combining capacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safe mushroom identification
rubrics_metrics.description: Certain genera are safer to eat: boleti (bolete-type mushrooms) are safer than many others, especially those that arise on trees, with long stalks, thin/ crisp caps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Harvest fungi typically found in woods or near specific stones, avoid those without a true root/radix (author asserts fungi always have a root). Prefer boleti with the described morphology; be cautious of other genera and of fungi growing from corrupt/unknown substrates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Propagation via dung/manuring for strong seedlings
rubrics_metrics.description: Planting in warm, humid dung (e.g., goat dung) or mixing dung into planting holes accelerates germination and produces vigorous seedlings and more seed/fruit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Female plants in warmed pots/situations produce more seed and fruit; transplanting into holes filled with warmed/fermented dung can produce rapid, abundant growth. Use this for species where stronger germination is desired (e.g., apium, porri, lactuce).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserving by cold (ice/snow) and storage location
rubrics_metrics.description: Large blocks of ice/snow or exposure to glacier-like cold preserve fruits best; cool, shaded caverns, cellars, or exposure among marble/crystalline structures prolong preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Store fruits in icy cellars or among ice/snow; region matters—some mountain sites provide long-lasting ice. The larger and longer the initial freezing process, the denser and longer-lasting the ice and the better the preservative effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Refrigerating water and wines with saline halinitrum
rubrics_metrics.description: To achieve maximum coldness in liquids, add halinitrum (salt-like substance) in measured fractions while stirring slowly in a 'pistilli' form until the liquid reaches maximal cold.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Procedure: take three parts liquid, add two thirds then slowly stir, then add half a residual part of halinitrum, repeat slow stirring until extreme cold is reached. Afterward, halinitrum can be reboiled out if required. The method is preferred to mere ice in certain cases but ice/snow remains superior in some general contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degree of cooking/processing for preserving flavors
rubrics_metrics.description: Fruits/herbs intended for preserving with honey or sugar should be cooked to a moderate dryness—not too much—so they best retain and combine flavors and odors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the preserved goods become too dry they do not absorb other flavors well; aim for moderate cooking and then drying in shade before final sugar infusion to obtain optimal taste and aroma retention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for preventing spoilage during collection/handling
rubrics_metrics.description: Harvest and process perishables promptly and avoid contamination: remove pedicels where rot begins, avoid humid/tainted storage, and protect from fermentative growth by proper boiling/drying/salting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pick fruits at appropriate ripeness, avoid damaged parts (especially near pedicels), boil or treat with vinegar/oil/salt, dry in shade or bake lightly, and store in cool, dry containers. For fruits that tend to putrefy, roast or treat before storage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bait and trap selection for birds and fish
rubrics_metrics.description: Use baits with attractive odor and taste (anise, cumin, coffee, certain oriental berries) and employ traps/reticula tailored to species: nets and decoys for birds, rods and reticulum placements for crabs/cancer and fish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For ducks and fowl use 'cicuratas' and boiled baits near enclosed waters; for fish use intestines or frog bodies placed in order by crevices and align rods and nets along likely channels so fish enter and cannot escape. Ensure bait has the right smell and is placed where the species expects food (current lines, edges).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use and selection of aromatics in preserves and medicine
rubrics_metrics.description: Aromatic additives (vinegar, oil, garyophyllus/clove, pepper) alter heat/humor qualities and preserve tinctures/foods: vinegar cuts grease and preserves flavor; oil keeps substances 'fat and dry'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Add vinegar to moderate sweetness and counteract heat; use olive oil for fatty, drying preservation; combine aromatics prudently so that odors are harmonious and do not overpower. When preparing medicinals, remember that different aromatics suit different temperaments and aims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparing pigments/imprints from plants
rubrics_metrics.description: To imprint plant colors/figures onto leather/paper use fresh plant juices, press onto paper, fix with carbon/char, and remove excess with cotton; lacquers or wax ('cera') can be added for finish.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technique: apply fresh green plant juice to paper (charta), press (impressio), then use charcoal and soot to fix color and add 'lacrymam' (a fixative). Use a covering layer to compress and let dry; for more durable effects add wax/varnish ('cera') and bind between boards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fungal generation rule: substrate/root necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Fungi generation depends on substrate and a root; the author asserts no fungus arises without a root and that fungi are produced by mixtures of similar/dissimilar matters and changes in location/nutrition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating fungi origin and edibility, inspect substrate and root attachment; generation is affected by contamination, local nutrition, and vessel/cordage conditions. Use this to judge likely safety and origin of mushrooms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling and curing of cooked meats/fish for storage
rubrics_metrics.description: Cooked meats and fish should be carefully drained, dried in shade, re-oiled or dressed with vinegar/white salt, and rotated periodically to prevent corruption; certain leaves (lauri, myrtus) improve preservation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: After cooking, press/extract liquid, dry in shade for an hour or more, then season with white vinegar or salt; turn items every few days. For fish, laurel leaves and myrtle can correct corrupted water and improve taste; avoid storage in warm, stagnant vessels.
